premises.text: Conventional databases are rigid and siloed so related app data cannot live together
premises.evidence_span: applications that had related data no longer were forced to store it into unrelated databases

premises.text: FluidDB is a shared writable database where any application can add information to anything without permission
premises.evidence_span: It's a shared database for applications

premises.text: Independent apps storing into FluidDB enable unanticipated cross-app queries combining their data
premises.evidence_span: I've combined data in an unanticipated way from three independent but related applications

premises.text: Provides a shared writable object for everything—platform for the web of things
premises.evidence_span: FluidDB gives you a shared, writable object for everything

value.text: Related information lives together so apps and people can add data without asking permission—making data more useful
value.evidence_span: they're choosing to store their information into a place that makes it more valuable, because it's more useful

secondary_value.text: Writable, social future of data where applications do not own the final word
secondary_value.evidence_span: The future of data is a writable future

causal_links.evidence_span: because it stores data into FluidDB, it's just the beginning
forced to store it into unrelated databases
none of them had to ask permission to put that information into FluidDB

notes: Tickery/TunkRank/We Met At demos folded as cascade illustrating one shared-DB mechanism (§4.1.7). 'Future of data' vision recorded as secondary_value not premises (§4.1.4). Funding anecdote excluded (§4.2). Wikipedia analogy is framing. Two domains—not a triad.
